headline: NZ Budget Advances as Abuse-in-Care Redress Bill Passes Amid Fierce Debate
summary: Parliament advanced the Government’s 2026 Budget after a debate over household hardship, child poverty, jobs and public spending, while an Opposition no-confidence amendment was defeated. MPs also passed a contested abuse-in-care redress bill and began debating changes to workplace safety law, with critics warning the proposals could weaken protections. Disputes over public-service staffing and commercial activity on conservation land added to the day’s political tension.

topicSummaries.topic: Budget 2026 Wins Second-Reading Vote Amid Cost-of-Living Dispute
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The Budget sets spending priorities for public services and infrastructure, while its choices affect household support, employment and the Government’s fiscal outlook.
topicSummaries.content: The Appropriation (2026/27 Estimates) Bill, which authorises the Government’s planned spending, passed its second reading by 67 votes to 54; an Opposition no-confidence amendment was defeated by 67 votes to 54. Finance Minister Nicola Willis and other Government MPs defended the Budget’s focus on fiscal restraint and targeted investment, citing Treasury forecasts of 2.7 percent average growth over four years, 220,000 additional jobs and a return to surplus in 2028-29. Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori argued that households were bearing the costs of the approach, pointing to job losses, business liquidations, housing pressures and gaps in support. The debate also covered investment in health, schools, trade training, social housing and regional infrastructure.

keyExchanges.speaker: Megan Woods (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: This was this Government’s last chance in this Budget to prove to New Zealanders that they got it—whether that be New Zealand households that are sitting at the table thinking: “How am I going to pay my bills? What am I going to do when the car breaks down? How am I going to make ends meet?” or New Zealand businesses that are struggling to stay afloat. They did not deliver this in Budget 2026.

keyExchanges.speaker: Nicola Willis (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Ultimately, when a Government puts a Budget together, it has to make choices.

topicSummaries.topic: Labour Cites 170,000 Children in Material Hardship
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Material hardship can mean children miss out on essentials such as food, warm housing, clothing and healthcare, with consequences for their wellbeing and education.
topicSummaries.content: During the Budget debate, Labour MP Jan Tinetti cited figures released alongside the Budget showing nearly 170,000 children were experiencing material hardship—50,000 more than three years earlier—and said the country was not on track to meet its 2028 targets. She argued the figures reflected the effects of Government policy and called for greater action to reduce poverty. Government MPs defended the Budget’s spending priorities and emphasis on targeted support, while opposition MPs also raised food insecurity, housing costs and access to healthcare as concerns for families.

topicSummaries.topic: Abuse-in-Care Redress Bill Passes Despite Survivor-Access Dispute
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The law establishes how survivors of abuse in State care can seek financial and other redress, including how claims are handled for some people with serious convictions.
topicSummaries.content: The House passed the Redress System for Abuse in Care Bill at its third reading. The Government said the legislation creates a more consistent process, extends eligibility to people abused in State mental-health inpatient settings between 1993 and June 2022, and includes assistance accessing care records. It also establishes a presumption against financial redress for survivors convicted of specified serious offences and sentenced to more than five years, while allowing applications for an independent redress officer to review that presumption; other forms of redress remain available. Labour and the Greens opposed the bill, arguing it falls short of the Royal Commission’s call for an independent, survivor-led system and could place additional hurdles on some survivors. ACT defended the approach as a compromise that balances survivors’ claims with the interests of victims of later offending.

keyExchanges.speaker: Willow-Jean Prime (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: This redress system bill does not take responsibility. It side-steps it.

keyExchanges.speaker: Laura McClure (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: Support and help—100 percent, yes—but not financial redress.

topicSummaries.topic: Workplace Safety Bill Advances Amid Pike River Concerns
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Changes to workplace safety duties could affect how employers manage hazards and the protections workers rely on to avoid injury or death.
topicSummaries.content: Workplace Relations and Safety Minister Brooke van Velden moved the Health and Safety at Work Amendment Bill to its second reading, saying it would reduce duplication and focus employers on risks most likely to cause serious harm. The proposal includes different duties for smaller businesses and changes to how workplace risks are assessed. Labour and Green MPs said the changes could leave workers less protected, particularly in small businesses, and cited opposition from submitters and concerns raised by Pike River families. New Zealand First MP Mark Patterson offered what he called “tepid support”, saying the bill had drawn extensive criticism and that his party wanted further discussion with the Minister and coalition partners before the committee stage. The debate was interrupted at adjournment, with no second-reading vote recorded.

keyExchanges.speaker: Brooke van Velden (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: This bill does not lower standards. It strengthens the system by making it clearer and more practical.

keyExchanges.speaker: Mark Patterson (New Zealand First)
keyExchanges.quote: If there has ever been a case that we step back and reassess after listening to feedback to the select committee, this is it.

topicSummaries.topic: Ministers Give No Full Assurance on Public-Service Job Cuts
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Reductions in government staffing could affect both public-sector employees and the availability of services people rely on.
topicSummaries.content: Labour MP Camilla Belich challenged the Government over plans to reduce public-service roles, saying the Budget involved 9,000 job cuts and asking which services or positions would be affected. Public Service Minister Paul Goldsmith said agencies were assessing possible staff reductions and that the Government wanted to protect frontline services, but he did not rule out cuts to specific functions raised in questions, including suicide prevention, search and rescue and the Labour Inspectorate. He said teachers, doctors, nurses and police were outside the staffing exercise and argued that agencies should focus on back-office efficiencies.

keyExchanges.speaker: Camilla Belich (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: The people who do suicide prevention; the people who do search and rescue; the people who work in the Labour Inspectorate to investigate crimes against vulnerable workers; the people who work for Oranga Tamariki’s contact centre, the contact centre where people call to alert authorities that children are in danger. I asked Ministers to rule out cuts to all of those important jobs

keyExchanges.speaker: Paul Goldsmith (National)
keyExchanges.quote: We’re going through a process, as a Government, of asking Government departments to reverse some of the hiring spree that went on under the previous Government, and we’re giving them the ability to do that, but we’ve also sent a clear signal that when they’re doing that, they shouldn’t be focusing on the front line; they should be focusing elsewhere.

topicSummaries.topic: Conservation Land Proposal Fuels Debate Over Commercial Use
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Changes to how conservation land may be used or transferred could affect public access, environmental protection and the management of natural areas.
topicSummaries.content: Green co-leader Marama Davidson pressed the Government over a proposal to allow some conservation land to be disposed of or used for commercial activity, citing public opposition and concerns about the Department of Conservation’s role. Foreign Affairs Minister Winston Peters, answering for the Prime Minister, said the proposal did not mean 60 percent of the conservation estate would be sold and described possible transfers as including sites such as gravel pits or historic buildings. He said the bill was before a select committee and could be changed. The exchange followed opposition arguments in the Budget debate that cuts to the Department of Conservation could undermine its ability to protect the estate.

keyExchanges.speaker: Marama Davidson (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Does he recognise the significant public opposition to this bill, including the 24,000 people who submitted on this bill just on the weekend alone, and if so, will he reassure New Zealanders by ruling out the sale of conservation land and putting this bill in the bin?

keyExchanges.speaker: Winston Peters (New Zealand First)
keyExchanges.quote: The reality is there are, for example—take the Belvedere Hall. If an Historic Places Trust group of people say, “We wish to look after that hall ourselves. It’s 142 years old.”, why would that sale be adverse to New Zealanders’ interests?

conclusion: The Government secured progress for its Budget and redress legislation, but opposition over household hardship, survivor protections, workplace safety and the future of public services remained unresolved.
